task.goal: Make a nonprofit's public FAQ easier to update when policy answers change.
hard_constraints: One editor has two hours weekly and a static website; no new content system.
Do not publish an answer without a named source and review date.
Track stale answers, conflicting pages and reader failures to find a current answer.
task.available_resources: Existing FAQ files and policy memo archive.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One canonical answer per policy question
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make each policy answer live in exactly one existing static FAQ location. Replace repeated answers elsewhere with descriptive links to that location. This changes the maintenance problem: a policy revision requires one substantive edit instead of several synchronized edits.

For every answer, show the named source document, its archive identifier or date, and the date the editor checked the answer against it. A scheduled next-review date can also support maintenance. If the archive does not support an answer, publish only a notice that the answer is awaiting verification, with a contact route; do not infer policy.

Keep a small spreadsheet or text register beside the existing files: question, canonical URL, source, review date, next review, and known pages that repeat or contradict it. Add a visible “Couldn’t find a current answer?” email link using an existing monitored address. Record the reader’s question and starting page, without retaining unnecessary personal details.

Use the weekly two hours for 20 minutes reviewing new memos and reader reports, 70 minutes updating affected canonical answers and removing conflicting copies, and 30 minutes checking overdue entries and links. Begin with the most frequently changing questions; record remaining duplication as an explicit backlog.

This assumes the editor can edit relevant static pages and access a monitored inbox. External copies remain outside direct control. Links may also make readers take an extra step, so descriptive link wording matters.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot five questions with known repetition. Compare updating one changed policy through canonical answers against the current duplicate-edit process, recording time and missed contradictions. Ask three unfamiliar readers to locate the current answer from different starting pages and identify its source and review date. Inspect the register for overdue answers and unresolved conflicts. The mechanism fails its initial check if duplication remains unnoticed or readers cannot reliably reach the canonical answer.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Trace policy changes to affected answers
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep the FAQ’s current structure, but maintain a lightweight dependency register connecting policy memos to every public passage they support. The primary mechanism is change propagation: when a memo changes, the register supplies a concrete checklist of affected answers and potentially conflicting pages.

Use a spreadsheet or plain text file with one row per answer or policy-bearing passage: page location, question, named source and specific section, last review date, next review date, and status. Each published answer also displays its named source and last review date. A new or revised memo triggers review of all linked rows. Search the existing website files for distinctive terms and old wording to catch passages missing from the register. Record contradictory pages until corrected; record unsupported answers for removal or replacement with an awaiting-verification notice.

Spend 25 minutes weekly inspecting archive additions, 65 minutes applying the highest-impact changes, and 30 minutes checking overdue rows, unresolved conflicts, and reader reports. Add a plain email feedback link asking what answer the reader sought and where they looked; log unresolved searches in the same register. Those reports trigger dependency and navigation checks.

This uses the existing files and memo archive without changing publishing infrastructure. It assumes archive changes can be identified and sources are sufficiently specific to map to answers. Initial mapping takes time, so inventory a manageable section each week and mark unmapped sections explicitly. The largest uncertainty is whether the register can stay complete within the editor’s time budget.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Map one FAQ section, then select an archived policy revision whose affected passages can be independently inspected. Compare register-guided review with a simple keyword search of the same files. Count affected passages missed and minutes required, without assuming either method is complete. Submit one simulated failed-search report and verify that it enters the register and leads to a concrete check. Reject or simplify this approach if maintaining dependencies consumes more time than it saves or repeatedly misses relevant pages.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Time-limited answers with a weekly renewal queue
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Give every answer a defined period of validity for publication, then use a weekly renewal queue to prevent unsupported answers from remaining indefinitely. The mechanism is a publication gate: an answer stays available as current guidance only while its documented review remains within its assigned interval.

Add a named source, last review date, and next review date to each answer. Use shorter intervals for policies known to change frequently and longer intervals for stable material; choose initial intervals provisionally because the archive may not establish change frequency. Maintain a plain register sorted by next review date, with columns for conflicting pages and reader failures. Every weekly session also checks new policy memos, which can trigger immediate review before an answer’s scheduled date.

Allocate 20 minutes to new memos and reader feedback, 75 minutes to renewing or replacing due answers, and 25 minutes to finding contradictory wording and updating the register. If an answer cannot be verified, replace its substantive guidance with a clear verification-pending notice and an existing contact route. A visible email link collects reports of missing, confusing, or apparently outdated answers. Log these reports even when the answer is technically current.

This requires only edits to static files and a small register. It assumes the editor can sustain weekly publication and that a contact route already exists. Expiration is handled manually, so missed sessions remain a risk. Review intervals cannot guarantee correctness between checks, and withdrawing answers can reduce usefulness; track pending notices as a backlog, not as successful maintenance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot a small FAQ section for four weekly sessions, using intervals short enough to exercise renewal. Compare it with a similar section maintained by the existing routine. Inspect overdue published answers, editing time, conflicting passages, and questions left without useful guidance. Ask three readers to distinguish current guidance from a pending notice and find the contact route. The approach fails if renewals exceed the available time, overdue answers remain presented as current, or withdrawals create more unresolved reader failures than the workflow can address.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use source excerpts to reduce policy rewriting
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace selected paraphrased FAQ answers with short, exact excerpts from the policy memo archive, preceded by a plain-language question and a brief statement of who and what the excerpt covers. The primary mechanism is reducing translation work: the editor selects and checks authoritative wording instead of repeatedly reconstructing policy explanations. Keep existing static files and navigation; no new publishing system is required.

Every published answer must display the named source memo, its date and section, and the date the editor reviewed it. Include any conditions or exceptions needed to make the excerpt accurate. If the archive does not establish which conflicting memo governs, replace the substantive answer with a verification-pending notice rather than choosing a policy interpretation.

Keep a plain-text work log alongside the FAQ files. Record each answer’s location, source, review date, next check, and unresolved issues under three labels: stale answer, conflicting page, and reader could not find current guidance. Add an email feedback link using an existing monitored address, asking which question the reader sought and where they looked. Search existing site files for wording from superseded excerpts and related terms whenever a policy changes; log conflicting passages until resolved.

Budget the weekly two hours as 20 minutes checking archive changes and feedback, 70 minutes replacing affected excerpts and correcting conflicting pages, and 30 minutes checking stale entries and reader navigation failures. Start with a small section and expand within that allowance.

This assumes the editor can identify authoritative memos, quote them publicly, and access an existing feedback inbox. It works best when memo passages are short and understandable. Dense, confidential, or interdependent policies may make excerpts unsuitable; their readability and completeness remain unproven.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype three excerpt-based answers and compare them with three manually checked paraphrases covering the same policies, all carrying sources and review dates. Use one archived revision to rehearse an update; record editing time, omitted conditions, and remaining contradictory passages. Ask three unfamiliar readers to find an answer and apply it to a scenario involving an exception. Log a simulated failed-search report and an intentionally overdue review. Reject the approach if excerpts save no editing time, obscure policy conditions, or prevent readers from identifying applicable current guidance.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Maintain policy answers as explicit decision tables
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
For policies whose answers depend on eligibility, dates, or exceptions, replace branching FAQ prose with small decision tables in the existing static pages. Each row states a reader’s circumstances, the applicable answer, and any exception. The mechanism is making policy branches explicit: a change to one eligibility condition becomes a bounded row edit, while overlapping or missing cases become easier to inspect. This could reduce the effort of checking prose that scatters conditions across several answers.

Use the existing memo archive to build one table at a time. Every substantive row must display its named source memo and section plus the date the editor reviewed it. Include effective dates where relevant. Publish a row only when its conditions and answer are supported; unresolved cases receive a verification-pending notice without speculative guidance. Use ordinary HTML tables with clear headers and short introductory instructions; no new content system or generator is needed.

Keep a plain-text issue list beside the files with three categories: stale rows, conflicting pages, and readers unable to find current guidance. Record the affected location, discovery date, and next action. When editing a table, search existing files for the changed condition and previous answer, and log contradictions until corrected. Add a feedback email link if an existing monitored address is available; otherwise, reader checks during the weekly session supply failure reports.

Reserve 20 minutes weekly for new memos and reports, 70 for table updates and conflicting pages, and 30 for overdue reviews and one reader-path check. Initial conversion must fit that same allowance, starting with one small policy family.

This assumes policies can be expressed as a manageable set of cases. Interacting conditions can make tables unwieldy, and a complete-looking table can conceal missing cases. Source interpretation and accessibility still require judgment.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype one table for a policy with an exception. Compare it with the existing prose after checking both against the same memos. Rehearse one archived policy change and record editing time and missed affected passages. Ask three readers to find and apply guidance for an ordinary case, an exception, and an unsupported case. Inspect source and review-date coverage, and log any failed lookup. Reject the approach for that policy if it takes longer to maintain without improving case accuracy, or if readers confidently choose incorrect rows.

EXPAND.title: Publish narrowly framed policy excerpts
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce the interpretation needed to maintain an answer: pair each question with the shortest policy-memo excerpt that directly answers it, plus a brief explanation of whom it covers. Updating becomes selecting and checking authoritative wording rather than rewriting a paraphrase. Unlike the prior canonical-answer route, this reduces the substantive editorial work even where there is only one FAQ page.

Start with five questions whose answers are explicitly stated in the archive. Show the named memo, section, policy effective date when specified, and editor review date beside every excerpt. Include qualifications necessary to preserve its meaning. Link to the memo only if it is already public; otherwise provide its identifying details without exposing restricted material. Do not use an excerpt when its authority, scope, or relationship to another memo is unclear. Replace unsupported guidance with a verification-pending notice and an existing contact route, if available.

Keep a plain-text worklist recording stale excerpts, conflicting public passages, and reader failures to find a current answer. A small email link can collect failures if a monitored address exists; otherwise use brief observed reader checks. Each week, spend 25 minutes checking archive changes and reports, 65 minutes replacing affected excerpts and correcting conflicts, and 30 minutes reviewing the worklist and navigation.

This needs only the existing files and archive. It assumes some memos contain clear, public-safe language. Legalistic wording or scattered exceptions may make excerpts harder to understand; those questions remain unsuitable for this method.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor owns a two-week, five-question trial within the weekly time limit. Prepare excerpt answers and ordinary sourced paraphrases for the same questions. Compare editing time after one archived revision and ask three readers to answer the relevant practical questions and locate current guidance. Inspect source dates, omitted qualifications, conflicting pages, and the failure log. Stop expanding if excerpts save no editing time, expose inappropriate material, or cause more misunderstandings than paraphrases. Record unsuitable questions rather than forcing them into the format.

EXPAND.title: Make policy conditions explicit in a decision table
EXPAND.proposal:
For questions whose answer varies by eligibility, location, application date, or another documented condition, replace ambiguous prose with a small static decision table. The mechanism is explicit partitioning: readers and the editor can see which policy applies to each case. This addresses apparent contradictions caused by missing scope, which a canonical answer or memo-to-page register can leave unresolved.

Choose one question with a manageable number of policy-supported branches. Extract only conditions that actually affect its answer. Give every answer row a named source, section, and review date; show effective dates separately where documented. Include a clearly labeled unresolved branch when the archive does not establish an answer. That branch supplies no inferred policy and points to an existing contact route, if available. If the table requires many interacting conditions, retain a narrow statement of the supported cases and mark the rest unresolved.

Maintain the table directly in the existing FAQ file. Keep a companion text checklist containing stale rows, other pages with incompatible or insufficiently scoped wording, and observed or reported failures to find the applicable answer. During the weekly two hours, allow 30 minutes for archive and reader intake, 60 for table and conflicting-page edits, and 30 for checking branch coverage and unresolved cases.

This assumes the archive identifies the relevant distinctions clearly. No rules engine or new publishing system is needed. The main risks are omitted conditions and a table that becomes harder to maintain than prose. Branches express documented policy; they do not authorize the editor to resolve policy disputes.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor runs a two-week trial on one conditional question. Compare the table with a sourced prose answer using several documented cases, including an exception and an unsupported case. Ask three readers to find the applicable guidance. Measure correct selection, unresolved searches, update time, and missed conditions after an archived revision. Stop expanding if the table exceeds the weekly budget, creates unsupported certainty, or offers no improvement over prose after its extra maintenance is counted.

EXPAND.title: Add a reader-language route to existing answers
EXPAND.proposal:
Keep the existing answer locations but add a compact static index using the words readers use to describe their problems. The mechanism changes retrieval: a current, maintained answer becomes easier to find without requiring readers to know the nonprofit’s policy terminology. This targets a gap in the prior dependency-register route, which can keep answers accurate while leaving them difficult to discover.

Begin with one FAQ section. Collect phrases from existing reader reports, if available, or from brief checks in which readers describe what they would look for. Map several useful phrases to each relevant answer using descriptive links and existing page anchors. Label links by scope where needed, such as applicant type or policy period. The index contains navigation labels rather than duplicated policy guidance. Any explanatory text that does state policy must carry its own named source and review date.

Before including an answer, verify its source and review date against the archive. Unsupported answers receive a pending notice instead of substantive guidance. Keep a small text register of overdue answers, conflicting pages, and failed journeys, recording the sought question and starting page. Use reader failures to revise index wording and link placement, while memo changes trigger answer and scope-label checks.

Reserve 30 weekly minutes for archive checks, 50 for substantive corrections, 25 for navigation and failure reports, and 15 for overdue and conflict review. This requires ordinary static-file editing. It assumes discovery is a material problem; without reader observations that remains uncertain. Too many synonyms can create clutter, so keep only labels that resolve an observed or plausible ambiguity.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor trials an index for six existing questions over two weeks. Give three unfamiliar readers comparable lookup tasks with and without the index, alternating the starting version. Compare successful arrival at current guidance, time spent, wrong-scope selections, and maintenance minutes. Inspect every destination for its source and review date and log failures even when the answer exists. Stop expanding if lookup success does not improve or index upkeep displaces necessary policy corrections within the two-hour budget.

EXPAND.title: Use a local prepublication check for mechanically detectable errors
EXPAND.proposal:
Add a small local checking script to the existing static-file workflow. Its mechanism is automatic enforcement of publication requirements and detection of known obsolete wording before an edit goes live. The prior dependency register relies on the editor remembering and executing checks; this route makes a limited set of checks repeatable. It does not determine which policy is authoritative.

For a bounded FAQ section, mark answer blocks consistently in the existing files. Each block includes a named source, source identifier, and review date. Store a small plain-text list of review deadlines and phrases known to have been superseded. Before publishing, run a read-only script that reports missing metadata, overdue answers, broken internal answer links, and occurrences of those obsolete phrases across website files. Missing source or review date blocks publication of the affected answer; overdue or phrase matches require editorial inspection rather than automatic deletion.

The editor checks the archive, makes supported changes, reviews the report, and publishes through the existing process. Unverifiable answers become pending notices. Keep unresolved stale items, suspected conflicts, and reader lookup failures in a plain-text issue list. Collect failures through an existing monitored address or occasional observed lookup checks; software cannot infer them from static files alone.

A first setup session must fit inside two hours, so cover only a few consistently formatted answers initially. Later weeks allocate 25 minutes to intake, 65 to editing, and 30 to checks and unresolved issues. This assumes an existing local scripting runtime and sufficient technical ability. Otherwise the implementation cost may outweigh its benefit. Source metadata can be present yet wrong, and paraphrased contradictions may escape detection.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor owns a one-session prototype on copied files, with no production changes required. Seed a missing source, missing review date, overdue answer, obsolete phrase, and a semantic contradiction using different wording. Compare the script plus editorial review with a manual checklist, counting missed defects and total setup and review time. Confirm that reader failures still enter the issue list independently. Stop if setup exceeds two hours, supported edits are routinely blocked by false alarms, or the combined process offers no practical benefit over the checklist. Treat the undetected semantic contradiction as a stated coverage limit.

EXPAND.title: Canonical answers with interruption-safe retirement of duplicates
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the prior “One canonical answer per policy question” route. Keep one substantive FAQ answer per question, replace repeated guidance with descriptive links, and display the named source, source identifier and review date. The added mechanism closes an interruption gap: changing the canonical answer must not leave known conflicting copies presented as current until a later session.

The editor keeps a plain-text register containing the canonical URL, source, review date, next review, duplicate locations, stale items and reader lookup failures. For each changed policy, first identify affected copies using the register and a search of existing files. Prepare the verified canonical answer and replacement links together. Publish them in one existing deployment if supported. Otherwise, first replace known conflicting copies with neutral verification-pending notices, then publish the verified answer and restore descriptive links. Record the last completed action so an interrupted session resumes from the actual public state.

Use 25 weekly minutes for new memos and reader reports, 70 for complete question-level updates, and 25 for overdue items and unresolved conflicts. Start fewer updates when a safe completion cannot fit. An unsupported answer becomes a pending notice rather than remaining substantive guidance. Collect lookup failures through an existing monitored contact route, if available, or brief observed lookup checks.

This requires access to the relevant static files and identifiable policy sources. Compared with ordinary canonicalization, it adds temporary notices and publication coordination but reduces the period when known conflicting guidance remains public. If a conflicting page cannot be edited, record its location and place a scoped correction on the controlled FAQ; resolution remains incomplete. Source ambiguity prevents substantive publication.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor pilots three repeated questions within two weekly sessions. Use an archived revision and interrupt a copied-file update between publication steps. Inspect whether the recorded state supports safe resumption and whether any known conflicting answer remains presented as current. Compare total editing and recovery time with the original canonical-answer procedure. Ask three readers to find current guidance from different starting pages; record lookup failures, pending notices, stale answers and unresolved conflicts. Stop expanding if the procedure exceeds two hours weekly or temporary notices cannot be cleared without displacing higher-priority corrections.

EXPAND.title: Dependency tracking with a source-authority hold
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the prior “Trace policy changes to affected answers” route. Preserve its memo-to-passage register and website searches, but add a consequential decision before propagating a revision: establish whether the new memo actually supersedes the source for each affected scope. A newer archive date alone does not establish authority, effective date or applicability.

For each answer, the editor records its location, named source and section, review date, next review and status. When a memo changes, use these links to identify affected passages. Check explicit supersession language, effective dates and relevant conditions. If the archive clearly establishes the replacement, update all affected passages and their public source and review dates. If the documents are compatible but apply to different cases, state the documented scope. If their relationship remains unresolved, replace the disputed guidance with a verification-pending notice and log the conflicting documents and public pages. The editor does not invent an authority hierarchy.

Keep unresolved decisions in the same register, including the last completed action, so interruption does not turn a tentative interpretation into a published answer. Reopen them when archive evidence resolves the conflict. Record overdue answers and reader failures through an existing monitored contact route or observed lookup checks.

Allocate 30 weekly minutes to archive intake and authority checks, 65 to affected-page corrections, and 25 to overdue items, conflicts and reader failures. Map one manageable section at a time. This needs only existing files and a text register. Compared with the original dependency workflow, it costs additional source-reading time and may temporarily withdraw useful guidance, but prevents mechanically spreading an unsupported interpretation. Ambiguous archives remain a real limitation.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor trials one mapped FAQ section over two weekly sessions. Inspect archived examples of explicit replacement, different scopes and an unclear relationship, if available; otherwise use clearly labeled hypothetical cases on copied files. Check that supported changes propagate, scope differences remain visible and ambiguity triggers a hold. Compare time and affected passages missed with the original register workflow. Inspect stale entries, conflicting pages, public source and review dates, and three reader lookup attempts. Stop expanding if source checks cannot fit the weekly limit or pending guidance accumulates faster than evidence permits resolution; retain the register for the bounded section.

EXPAND.title: Use public policy documents as the answer destination
EXPAND.proposal:
For suitable questions, remove the secondary policy rendition altogether. The FAQ becomes a question-to-document locator pointing directly to the exact section of an existing public policy memo. The working principle is to avoid maintaining a separate paraphrase whose wording can drift when policy changes. Unlike quoting excerpts or consolidating FAQ prose, the substantive guidance remains in its original public document.

The editor first checks whether the archive contains publicly accessible, authoritative documents with sufficiently clear sections and stable links. Pilot only questions where a reader can obtain a practical answer directly from such a section. Each FAQ entry displays the named source and the date the editor checked its authority, applicability and destination. Include only enough sourced scope information to select the appropriate document. Do not expose private memos or send readers to an undifferentiated archive.

Maintain a small text register of question, destination, named source, review date, next review, stale destinations, conflicting website passages and reader lookup failures. When a replacement memo appears, verify its applicability and change the destination rather than rewriting policy guidance. Correct conflicting passages on controlled pages. A missing, superseded or unclear destination becomes a pending notice until verified. If the document proves unsuitable, restore a verified, sourced FAQ answer; this route need not cover every question.

Use 25 weekly minutes for archive changes, 55 for destination and conflict corrections, and 40 for overdue checks and reader journeys. No new content system is needed. Feasibility depends on public document access and readability, which the supplied materials do not establish. Compared with a maintained FAQ paraphrase, this may reduce duplicated editorial work while shifting interpretation and navigation effort to readers.
EXPAND.experiment: The editor first inspects five candidate questions within one two-hour session. Stop this route immediately if no public, authoritative, directly usable destinations exist. For qualifying questions, compare locator entries with verified sourced paraphrases using three unfamiliar readers. Record correct practical answers, successful arrival at current guidance, time, wrong-scope selections and failures. Rehearse one archived replacement and inspect update minutes, stale links and conflicting pages. Continue only for questions where reduced maintenance justifies the observed reader burden; restore sourced paraphrases wherever readers cannot reliably use the documents.
